title: Trustworthy and High-Performance Question Answering for Electronic Health Records
text:
This project is interested in developing automatic question answering (QA) data and methods for
improving the usability of electronic health record (EHR) systems. Specifically we focus on trying
to balance the trustworthiness of our existing EHR QA system with the high-performance of state-
of-the-art QA based on large language models (LLMs).

title: Mapping of the intrinsic and extrinsic cerebellar connectome at ultra high resolution with expert neuroanatomical curation
text:
The human brain’s cerebellar connectome plays an important role in neurodevelopment and aging and has been
implicated in a large number of diseases. However, a complete map of the human cerebellar structural
connectome is still lacking due to multiple challenges that have thus far prevented comprehensive mapping of
its complex intrinsic and extrinsic pathways. We propose to address these challenges to create the most
comprehensive, anatomically curated maps of the intrinsic and extrinsic cerebellar connectome to date, which
will enable the study of the cerebellar connectome in health and disease.

title: Development of genetic approaches to study the organization and function of neocortical layer 1
text:
To comprehend the world around us, we must integrate the sensory information we receive from our sensory
organs with internal (“top-down”) information that provides context, behavioral saliency, emotions, memories,
predictions and expectations; this process is impaired in neurocognitive diseases such as autism and
schizophrenia. The outermost layer of the cortex, known as layer 1 (L1) is the main recipient of top-down
information, but the mechanisms by which it processes this information and integrates it with sensory signals are
poorly understood. This project will develop and validate new genetic tools to study a major neuronal population
in L1, and thereby will facilitate significant advances in our understanding of top-down sensory processing.

title: Nanohybrid Composites Minimize Antibiotic Resistant Infections
text:
Open fracture infections are increasingly difficult to treat due to growing antibiotic resistance. This application
outlines strategies to revive old antimicrobial agents by hybriding two materials with different dimensions at the
nanometer scale to increase antimicrobial properties and to reduce host toxicity.

title: Mechanisms of Stem Cell Memory in the Intestinal Epithelium
text:
Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) affects millions of people worldwide, yet many patients continue to relapse
even after achieving remission with current therapies, highlighting the urgent need for durable treatment
strategies. This project will investigate how intestinal stem cells retain a “memory” of prior inflammation that
alters their ability to regenerate the intestinal lining and restore barrier function. In the long term, this work
could lead to new therapeutic strategies including predictive biomarkers for restoring stem cell function,
enhancing mucosal healing, and preventing relapse in patients with IBD.

title: Novel Immunomodulators for Melanoma Therapy
text:
Our recently discovered small molecules are active against melanoma in mice models are and non-toxic. We
are proposing to test these leads compounds in additional models to test the feasibility of a new therapy
approach and determine their mechanism of action.

title: Functional interplay between Hippo and estrogen receptor ESR1
text:
Estrogen receptor gene (ESR1) plays a major role in development, tissue homeostasis, and
human cancer. The main goal of this proposal is to investigate the functional cross talk between
ESR1 and the Hippo pathway, which is known to play a major role in organ size control and
tumorigenesis. Completion of this project will not only address fundamental questions in ESR1
gene regulation and its role in Hippo biology, but also provide scientific basis for therapeutic
intervention of the Hippo pathway for ESR1 expressing cancers, such as breast cancer.

title: Biomaterial-Enhanced CAR-T/NK Cell Therapies for Glioblastoma.
text:
This research proposal focuses on enhancing the treatment of Glioblastoma (GBM) by integrating Chimeric
Antigen Receptor (CAR) T/NKT-cell therapy with translational biomaterials. The multidisciplinary team aims to
optimize CAR therapy and promote epitope spreading to better clear GBM. The ultimate goal is to transform
the eﬃcacy of CAR T/NKT cell therapies for GBM treatment.

title: Regulation of whole-body regeneration
text:
Select organisms are capable of regenerating an entirely new body during adulthood. This
research program aims to reveal the pathways and principles controlling whole body
regeneration in the planarian flatworm Schmidtea mediterranea and the distantly related acoel
Hofstenia miamia. These strategies seek to understand the conserved and uniquely evolved
spatial information systems and regulatory mechanisms that can enable regenerative growth.

title: Core E: Chemistry and Analytical Core (CAC)
text:
CHEMISTRY AND ANALYTICAL CORE
The overarching goal of Chemistry and Analytical Core (CAC) is to develop and apply ultra-sensitive and specific
analytical methods to measure metals (iAs, its species and other co-occurring contaminants) in environmental
and biological samples and characterize toxicant-induced adverse health effects via microbiome and
metabolomics approaches. These data provide critical research support for all UNC-SRP projects and promote
the integration of the UNC-SRP to better understand and protect the public from adverse health effects related
to Superfund chemicals.

title: A translational study of a synthetic lethality interaction of CD105 and androgen receptor signaling axis for castration-resistant prostate cancer patients
text:
Androgen receptor inhibition remains the most effective and among the least toxic interventions used to
effectively control advanced prostate cancers. Reversing and even preventing resistance is of the highest
importance to patients and clinicians given the lack of desirable, alternative treatment options. This proposal will
develop a novel means of regulating androgen receptor inhibition sensitivity by modulating biochemical signaling
in the microenvironment with a non-toxic agent that has entered clinical development.

title: HIV-1 Integrase Interactions with Viral RNA
text:
Our research focuses on elucidating structural and mechanistic foundations for HIV-1 integrase interactions with
the viral RNA genome, which is required for the formation of infectious virions. This non-catalytic function of HIV-
1 integrase is an important therapeutic target for a novel, investigational class of antiretrovirals called allosteric
integrase inhibitors or ALLINIs.

title: Child Health Research Career Development Award (K1-Renewal Yrs 31-35)
text:
The Child Health Research Career Development Award at Cincinnati Children’s Hospital Medical Center
has been in continuous operation for 31 years, fulfilling its mission of training young physician-scientists
who are seeking careers in pediatric research. The goal of the program is to provide a strong, well-
structured experience that will develop successful and independent investigators in child health who are
poised to become leaders in their chosen field.

title: The role of myelination in cortical circuit function and motor behavior
text:
The neural mechanisms underlying motor and cognitive impairments in multiple sclerosis (MS) patients are
largely unknown. This project uses novel synthesis of approaches in oligodendrocyte biology (with three-photon
imaging) and neurophysiology (with high-density neuropixels), to evaluate how myelin loss affects motor coding
and kinematic output in behavior.

title: Computational Chemistry and Bioinformatics Research Core
text: Core Summary The Glycoscience Center of Research Excellence (GlyCORE) Core 3, Computational Chemistry and Bioinformatics Research Core (CCBRC) at the University of Mississippi (UM), will perform advanced and state- of-the-art computations across a range of topics to support glycoscience research, with the ultimate objective to establish a self-sustaining Computational Research Core to advance glycoscience research in the Mid-South region. Glycoscience research frequently involves bioinformatics analysis and computational studies of complex glycans (including glycosaminoglycans) and exploration of their roles in various biological functions. Due to the structural diversity of complex glycans and varying sulfation patterns in glycosaminoglycans, identifying a likely structure and conformation of glycans experimentally is inherently challenging. Therefore, bioinformatics and computational chemistry approaches to address such challenges are essential in glycoscience. Glycobioinformatics tools and databases can be used to interpret LC/MS and MS/MS data and characterize glycan structures. Atomistic simulations can be used to model glycan ligands and N-/O-glycans attached to proteins, to assist assignment of sulfation patterns of glycosaminoglycans whose sulfation patterns have yet to be ascertained, and to provide in-depth insights into protein–glycan recognition mechanisms. Such efforts can enable the efficient design of biological experiments and the effective use of GlyCORE resources to speed up scientific discovery. The topmost priority for Phase II is to keep supporting the RPLs (Research Project Leaders) through collaboration and generating preliminary data to strengthen their external grant applications, aiding in career advancement for RPLs and their research teams. In addition to this, Phase II will focus on developing new computational and bioinformatics methods for glycoscience research, especially those required to support the current projects and to help CCBRC to thrive in the long run. CCBRC will continue focusing on making its capabilities known to other researchers in the Mid-South region, through meetings, glycoscience-oriented training, a dedicated webpage, and other outreach methods established by GlyCORE. The proposed work of CCBRC in Phase II will be to: support RPLs, PPLs (Pilot Project Leaders), and other glycoscience researchers in identifying computational approaches to assist them in their projects; provide training in computational methods for glycoscience; and develop computational methods for glycomics and structural and chemical glycobiology.

title: Noradrenergic mechanisms underlying stress-induced opioid reinstatement
text:
Opioid misuse is often initiated following the experience of a traumatic event in an attempt to alleviate the high
levels of arousal and anxiety that subsequently occur. The noradrenergic locus plays a major role in facilitating
such anxiety and is dysregulated in conditions including posttraumatic stress disorder that have a high rate of
comorbidity with substance misuse. The experiments proposed herein begin to address the underlying etiology
of stress- and substance use disorders by examining the underlying interactions between neuroimmune signaling
and norepinephrine release to identify novel targets for the treatment of these conditions.

title: BCM-TSU CURED Cancer Research Education Program (C-REP)
text:
CURED C-REP Project Narrative 
The CURED C-REP will provide an 8-weeks mentored cancer research experience that integrates Baylor College of Medicine (BCM) and Texas Southern University (TSU) infrastructures every summer followed by year- long outreach education activities that will increase the awareness, knowledge, and understanding of research, concepts, processes, and careers in cancer research/cancer health outcomes in a cohort of 20 TSU students. The proposed CURED C-REP will enhance cancer research education capacity at TSU, enhance workforce development, and improve BCM’s effectiveness in developing and sustaining research programs focused on cancer health outcomes.

title: Identification of Novel Innate Immune Checkpoint Receptors
text:
Cancer cells evade immune clearance by exploiting immune checkpoints, such as the "don’t-eat-me" signal
mediated by VCAM1. Our studies seek to identify the unknown VCAM1 receptor(s) on phagocytic cells and
determine their role in promoting immune tolerance in leukemia and mismatched stem cell transplantation. The
findings will inform new therapeutic strategies to enhance leukemia clearance and improve transplantation
outcomes, benefiting patients with hematologic malignancies.

title: Photoacoustic Imaging for Biophysical Physiological Indicators of Neonatal Intestinal Health and Necrotizing Enterocolitis
text:
Necrotizing enterocolitis is a devastating intestinal disease affecting premature infants that presents significant
clinical diagnostic difficulties due to the challenging disease and clinical setting. Advanced diagnostic imaging
modalities are not routinely available for use in the fragile NICU patient population at risk for NEC and
diagnostic confidence limits timely NEC diagnosis and effective medical management. This application
investigates the development of new advanced non-invasive imaging and analysis methods to characterize
biophysical physiological indicators of neonatal intestinal health and disease that presents significant
translational opportunity to improve the quality of care in the NICU.

title: Imaging Mass Cytometry Core
text: PROJECT SUMMARY - Core 3: Imaging Mass Cytometry Core The overall goal of the proposed CCHI U19 grant is to determine the mechanisms of mucosal immune responses to human-restricted enteric pathogens, S. typhi and Shigella, which to date remain significant global health concerns. To determine the limitations of current vaccine approaches and immune protection, we need to better understand the immunologic changes and the mechanisms thereof that are occurring systemically and locally within the gut mucosa. Leveraging our CCHI U19 team’s longstanding expertise in and unparalleled clinical infrastructure for evaluating the immune responses to these enteric pathogens, our proposed center seeks to understand the changes within major immune compartments, including T cells, B cells, and innate cells, upon clinical vaccinations and/or pathogen challenge. To accomplish this, we propose to phenotype the different immune cell subtypes and their functional states in-depth at the molecular level and interrogate how they are epigenetically regulated. Furthermore, to determine how the immune responses are orchestrated in situ within the mucosa, we propose to determine the spatial coordination among the immune cells in human mucosal biopsy samples and integrate this information with other molecular features. To enable synergy across all Research Projects, the Imaging Mass Cytometry Core will operate as a centralized service core, providing an imaging pipeline to be implemented on all biospecimens. The overarching purpose of the Imaging Mass Cytometry Core is, therefore, to generate high- parameter (30-40+ markers) spatial immune profiles with subcellular resolution for all three Research Projects. The Core will support the Research Project investigators with the expertise necessary to most optimally utilize imaging mass cytometry techniques. We established an efficient workflow to receive mucosal biopsy samples from University of Maryland and process them for imaging mass cytometry at Johns Hopkins. This Core will deliver the following: Aim 1, optimized and validated antibody panels suited for each Research Project along with the resulting multicolored quality-controlled images; and Aim 2, segmented single-cell data from the acquired images for compositional and neighbor/distance-based spatial analyses. The Core’s leadership and staff have demonstrated a strong track record of employing imaging mass cytometry to advance immunology studies, ensuring success of the proposed aims. The incorporation of our Core’s spatial analysis expertise will uniquely enhance the efforts of the proposed CCHI U19 to understand the immunologic barriers to effective protection and ultimately motivate new strategies for improved vaccine development.
